# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
## What the report says

This 24-month follow-up has two sources.

**Varden County, case-processing offices (7 v 7, randomised)**
- **Hours.** A second hours measure, active log-in time on the case system, was added to catch work not claimed on timesheets. Hours fell 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, relative to control.
- **Output per hour.** On the like-for-like timesheet measure, the gain fell from +12.5% at nine months to +9.8% at 24 months. On logs it is +8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8).
- **Output per FTE.** −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
- **Quality and retention.** Quality, sick-day and resignation differences are about as before.
- **Mechanism.** A mediation analysis registered at month 11 attributes 47% of the per-hour gain to fewer recurring meetings, 18% to lower fatigue, and leaves 35% unexplained.
- **Counter arm.** The county ended it at month 12 because of waiting times. Restoring service would have needed 12% more staff, at about 9% higher cost per contact.
- **Unplanned observation.** Two control offices cut meetings on their own initiative and gained 4.1% per hour against their own previous six months. The authors present this cautiously.

**Halden subset (14 of the 23 organisations with records)**
- Three reverted, with output indices of 88–91 at the time.
- The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour. The authors frame this as an upper bound for self-selected survivors.

**Bearing on the earlier papers**
- **Varga & Holm.** Varden at 24 months meets the standards they themselves set, and a gain remains. "Entirely an artifact" is therefore not supported.
- **The meta-analysis.** Its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so its "no decay" claim can't stand.

I checked the arithmetic:
- Varden: 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%.
- Halden: 34.9/40.3 = −13.4% and 96.8/86.6 = +11.8%.
- Counter arm: restoring output per FTE of −11.4% requires 1/0.886, or about 12.9% more staff, close to the stated 12%.

## Overall assessment

This report answers most of the questions the earlier documents left open, and mostly at the right weight.

**Now settled, as far as one employer can settle them:**
- **A real per-hour gain persists at two years under strict measurement.** The design is randomised, output comes from records, hours come from logs, and the horizon is 24 months.
- **It is smaller than early estimates and has probably faded somewhat.**
- **Varga & Holm's "entirely an artifact" claim is not supported.** Their month-ten extrapolation of energy back to baseline is directly contradicted by the 24-month result.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is undercut.** The authors checked the supplementary table and found its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. That was the composition question I had raised.
- **In coverage-bound work, reduced hours were not sustainable without more staff.** The county's decision is a stronger outcome than any rating scale.

The problems below concern the strength of individual claims, not the main result.

## Points worth addressing

**1. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
The body text says "survives a registered test," which is accurate. The Summary says "confirms." Three points support the weaker wording:
- **It is not an independent replication.** The test uses the same seven offices that generated the hypothesis. Registration before the 24-month outcomes rules out choosing the model after seeing results, but not the possibility that the original correlation was specific to these offices. Varga & Holm's complaint was that the finding "does not replicate," and that is still untested.
- **There are only 14 independent units.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but office-months are clustered within 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters, and the report should say how clustering was handled in the mediation model.
- **The identifying assumption is untestable here, as the authors acknowledge.** A plausible confounder is manager quality: better managers may both cut meetings and raise output.

"Supports" or "is consistent with" would match the evidence.

**2. Where did the baseline meeting figures come from?**
The nine-month report had meeting data only for month six. That was why "offices that cut meetings most" couldn't be supported at the time. This report gives baselines of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. If they were reconstructed from historical calendars, say so and describe how complete the reconstruction was. The baseline is what turns a level difference into a change, and the mediation result depends on it.

**3. A simple accounting check gives a different share from the mediation model.**
Assume log or timesheet hours include meeting time and that meetings close no cases.
- Non-meeting time: about 30.5 hours at baseline, about 29.2 hours at 24 months (after the difference-in-differences cut of about 3.3 meeting hours). That is a fall of about 4%.
- Output fell about 3.4%.
- Output per non-meeting hour is therefore roughly unchanged.

On this rough accounting, removing meeting time accounts for almost all of the per-hour gain, not 47%. That leaves little room for fatigue to raise the productivity of the hours that remain. The two estimates answer different questions: the mediation model works from variation across offices, while the accounting describes the average. Reconciling them would sharpen the mechanism claim considerably. Exactly what the system logs count, and whether they include time spent in meetings, matters for this.

**4. The control-office meeting figures may not reconcile.**
The two auditing control offices went from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. Yet the control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. Unless the averages are weighted by staff, or the offices are measured at different times, that implies the other five control offices increased their meeting time. Please check this.

**5. The control-arm meeting cuts slightly reduce the 24-month estimate.**
From month 15, two of seven control offices cut meetings and gained 4.1% per hour. This narrows the treated-versus-control difference in both the per-hour gain and the meetings mediator. The 8.5% is therefore, if anything, slightly understated, and the report should say so.

The 4.1% itself compares each office with its own previous six months. A difference-in-differences against the other five control offices over the same period is easy to compute and would remove secular trends. Offices that audited their meetings may also have done so because something was going wrong, so regression to the mean is possible.

**6. The decline from nine to 24 months is a point estimate.**
- The timesheet intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily, so the decline itself is not statistically established. "Consistent with some fading" in Section 3 is the right weight.
- Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" compares 12.5% on timesheets with 8.5% on logs. On the like-for-like timesheet measure, the decline is about a fifth (12.5 to 9.8).

**7. "Client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category.**
Two of the three Halden reverters were coverage-bound (hospitality and retail). The third, a marketing agency citing client deadlines, is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. That is a reversion in the category where the model is supposed to work. It is one case, but folding it into "coverage" hides it.

**8. Non-response adds a third layer of selection.**
Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. The nine that didn't may include more reverters. The upper-bound framing is right, but "survivors twice over" understates the selection: they completed the pilot, continued, and agreed to report.

**9. Sick days: is the schedule four days or five?**
At −27%, sick days are still reported without an interval, and the report still doesn't say whether staff work four days or five shorter days. This was raised for both earlier Varden reports and for Halden. With a four-day schedule, about 20 points of the fall would be mechanical.

**10. Novelty is reduced, not eliminated.**
A gain lasting two years is strong evidence against novelty in the ordinary sense. But staff knew their assignment and knew they were being evaluated throughout. Section 5 is correct that the re-analysis's conclusion fails. A single sentence noting that the gain persisted *under continued evaluation* would keep that claim at exactly its weight.

**11. The counter-arm cost estimate needs a short derivation.**
Twelve percent more staff raising cost per contact by 9% implies that non-staff costs are about a quarter of the total. That is plausible, but a sentence showing the calculation would let readers check it.

## Where the evidence stands across all five documents

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Supported: about 8.5% at 24 months in the strictest measurement; about 8–10% in better-designed studies |
| Persistence | Largely settled to two years in one controlled trial; modest fading likely but not established; beyond 24 months open |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported |
| Meta-analysis "no decay" | Not supported; its evidence came from inflated designs |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | Slightly below control (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2); mostly but not fully offset |
| Coverage-bound work | Settled: output falls, and service needs about 12% more staff to restore |
| Mechanism | Meetings supported in a registered test on the original offices; independent replication open; accounting suggests a share well above 47% |
| Gain without cutting hours | Open; suggested by two offices; needs a reorganise-only arm |

The last row points to the most valuable next study: a trial with a reorganise-only arm, which cuts meetings and approvals without reducing hours, alongside a reduced-hours arm and a control. It would separate the hours cut from the reorganisation it prompts, which neither the trial nor the review can do.

I can draft these as reviewer comments, or sketch the three-arm design.
